details:
**Pikes Peak**
A famous "fourteener" on the Front Range that overlooks Colorado Springs and can be seen from Denver. It is named for explorer Zebulon Pike, who tried and failed to reach its summit in 1806, and it is the most common late giveaway for the state.

**Denver, the "Mile High City"**
Colorado's capital and largest city, located on the South Platte River where Cherry Creek joins it, east of the Front Range. A step of the state capitol sits at exactly one mile (5,280 feet) above sea level, the city hosts a U.S. Mint, and its art museum added a titanium-clad wing designed by Daniel Libeskind in 2006. Aurora is a major suburb.

**Black Canyon of the Gunnison**
A deep, narrow, steep-walled gorge cut by the Gunnison River in Montrose County, now a national park. Its sheer cliff called the Painted Wall is the tallest cliff in Colorado, and parts of the canyon receive only about half an hour of direct sunlight a day.

**Mesa Verde National Park**
A park in southwestern Colorado that preserves cliff dwellings built by the Ancestral Puebloans. Its best-known structures are Cliff Palace, the largest cliff dwelling in North America, Spruce Tree House, and the Sun Temple, a ceremonial building thought to have had astronomical uses.

**Great Sand Dunes National Park**
A park in the San Luis Valley, next to the Sangre de Cristo Range, containing the tallest sand dunes in North America. It was upgraded from a national monument to a national park in 2004.

**Fourteeners and Mount Elbert**
"Fourteeners" are mountains with summits above 14,000 feet; Colorado has 58 of them, more than any other state. Mount Elbert in the Sawatch Range is the state's highest point, and Longs Peak is the best-known fourteener in Rocky Mountain National Park.

**Collegiate Peaks**
A group of fourteeners in the Sawatch Range named after universities, including Mount Harvard, Mount Yale, Mount Princeton, and Mount Oxford.

**Garden of the Gods and Colorado Springs**
Garden of the Gods is a park of red sandstone formations, such as the "Kissing Camels" and Steamboat Rock, just outside Colorado Springs. The city sits at the foot of Pikes Peak and is home to the U.S. Air Force Academy.

**Colorado River**
The river named for the state rises in Colorado's Rocky Mountains near La Poudre Pass, flows past Grand Junction (where the Gunnison joins it), and then runs through the Grand Canyon, Lake Powell, and Lake Mead on its way to the Gulf of California. Many tossups with this answer are actually about the river, and the name is also shared by rivers in Texas and Argentina.

**Front Range Urban Corridor**
The string of cities along the eastern base of the Rockies where most Coloradans live, linked by Interstate 25 (whose Denver stretch is called the "Valley Highway"). It includes Denver, Boulder (home of the flagship University of Colorado), Fort Collins, Greeley, Colorado Springs, and Pueblo.

**Aspen, Vail, and Breckenridge**
Colorado's famous mountain ski resort towns, which anchor the state's large ski and tourism industry.

**Golden**
A city just west of Denver that is home to the Colorado School of Mines and the headquarters and main brewery of Coors.

**Grand Junction and Grand Mesa**
Grand Junction is the main city of western Colorado, where the Gunnison River flows into the Colorado River. Nearby Grand Mesa is one of the largest flat-topped mountains in the world and should not be confused with the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde.

**Interstate 70, Eisenhower Tunnel, and Glenwood Canyon**
I-70 crosses the Rockies through the Eisenhower Tunnel, which passes under the Continental Divide at over 11,000 feet. Its stretch through Glenwood Canyon, built with cantilevered roadway and the Hanging Lake Tunnel, was one of the last major parts of the interstate system to be finished. Along I-70 is the tiny community of No Name.

**La Garita Caldera and Fish Canyon Tuff**
The La Garita Caldera in the San Juan Mountains was the source of one of the largest known volcanic eruptions in Earth's history, which deposited the huge rock layer called the Fish Canyon Tuff. The San Juans are also home to mining sites such as the Summitville Mine, and the state's gold-mining history includes Cripple Creek.
